constitution.intro: This constitution has 13 articles; article 3 (equity and risk) and article 9 (red lines) matter most. The numbers are starting suggestions and are tuned with journal data after 30 trades.

blocks.text: My first goal is survival, my second is profit. As long as there is capital, there is another chance.
A good trade is one taken by the rules, not one that made money. A loss within the rules is a cost of doing business.
The market is indifferent to me. Only three things are in my control: position size, exit point and my own behaviour.
Not trading is a decision too. No setup, no trade.
I keep two separate parts: the trading account (futures) and the long-term portfolio (spot). Their money is never mixed.
I trade only symbols on my written watchlist (at most 10 symbols); they must pass the article 4 liquidity filter.
Every trade has a type before entry: scalp, intraday or swing. The type and its target do not change after entry.
Risk per trade is 1% of trading-account equity (cap 2% only for an A+ setup). Risk means the dollar loss at the moment the stop is hit, not the margin amount.
Position size comes only from the formula below. Leverage is chosen after it to cover the required margin, not the other way round.
Position = Equity × Risk% ÷ SL distance%
Position value equals equity times risk percent, divided by the stop distance from entry in percent.

Default leverage is 3x to 5x and the absolute cap is 10x. If the stop is so close that keeping margin under 10% of equity would need leverage above 10 (at 1% risk, that is a stop closer than about 1%), I reject the trade; I raise neither leverage nor risk.
Margin per position is at most 10% of equity (usual target 5%) and the mode is always Isolated.
The liquidation price must be at least two times the stop distance away from the entry price.
The total risk of all open positions (if every stop is hit) is at most 3%, and I hold at most 3 positions at once. Same-direction positions on altcoins count as one correlated position.

Loss caps: daily 3% (stop until tomorrow), weekly 6% (stop until next week and review), drawdown 10% from the equity peak (stop for at least 7 days and return at risk 0.5% for 20 trades). Daily and weekly percentages are relative to equity at the start of that day or week. I measure peak and drawdown on an equity curve that holds trade P&L only; withdrawals and deposits are not drawdown.
After a win, size comes only from the formula. After a big win (above 3 times risk or 3% of equity in one day) I do not raise risk for up to 24 hours.

blocks.title: Worked example (hypothetical)
paragraphs: A long trade with 2,000 dollars of equity. Entry 100, stop 96 (a 4% distance) and target 108 (profit twice the loss).

1% risk is 20 dollars; so position value = 20 ÷ 0.04 = 500 dollars. At 5x leverage the margin is 100 dollars (5% of equity) and the liquidation price is about 80.5, roughly 4.9 times the stop distance. The 1% risk, sub-10% margin and liquidation-distance limits all hold.

If the stop is hit, the loss is 500 × 4% = 20 dollars, exactly the 1% risk. If the target is hit, the gross profit is 500 × 8% = 40 dollars; with an assumed 0.6 dollars of fees and funding, 39.4 dollars net remains, about 1.97 times the risk.

blocks.text: Before every entry, all eight items below must be "yes"; otherwise I do not trade.

items.text: The higher-timeframe trend is clear and in the trade's direction (counter-trend only with a written reason and half size).
Three timeframes checked (direction, setup, entry) and my entry is not right into higher-timeframe resistance or support.
The liquidity filter holds: 24h volume at least 100 million dollars and relative volume between 0.7 and 3.
Volume/price divergence checked; if present, entering in the direction of the big candle without confirmation is forbidden.
I am not within 30 minutes before to 60 minutes after a major economic event (Federal Reserve, inflation, employment).
Entry, stop loss, take profit and R:R (at least 1 to 1.5) are written before entry.
Position size comes from the formula and the article 3 limits hold (leverage at most 10, isolated, liquidation two times the stop distance, open risk at most 3%).
I am in good shape: not hungry, angry, lonely or tired, and not riding the excitement of a previous win or loss.

blocks.text: Entry with a Limit order in a zone I set in advance; scaling in with 2 to 3 orders is allowed.
Market orders are only for an emergency exit or an entry after a confirmed breakout. Chasing a candle is forbidden.
For breakouts I wait for a confirming candle close, because fake breakouts and stop hunts are common.
Stop loss and take profit are placed on the exchange at the moment of entry, not kept in my head. The stop sits behind structure plus about 0.5 to 1 ATR, not on a round number.
A missed trade is not a loss and I do not chase it.
At 1R to 1.5R I close 50% of the position and move the stop on the rest to entry (plus fees).
I hold the rest with a trailing stop (structure or ATR) to the target. Locking 50 to 70% of profit is only for moves above 3R.
The stop only moves toward profit; it is never moved further away or removed.
Averaging down on a losing position and adding margin to it are forbidden.
If the trade has not moved toward the target within 10 candles of the entry timeframe (default), I exit.
I do not turn a loss into a "long-term investment".
Watching means a live stop and target on the exchange, price alerts and set review hours. If I cannot monitor (sleep, travel, unstable internet), I do not open a position.
Profit is profit only once it is realized; open profit is just a number on the screen.
Each month 30% of realized profit (adjustable up to 50%) moves to spot or a personal wallet.
When I am deep in profit and want "more", I close part of it at once; greed is a signal.
Until the target or invalidation, I make no emotional decision between the two.
At most 3 trades a day. A 30 minute pause after each stop loss; after two consecutive stop losses, trading ends for the day.
Revenge trading and trading to recover a loss are forbidden.
Prayer rule: if I catch myself hoping or praying, it means I have no plan; I close half of the position.
Before every entry I record my emotion in the journal (calm, FOMO, greed, fear, revenge, bored).
I do not look for someone else to blame for a loss; first I check which rule I broke.
Breaking any of these means closing the trade at once and applying article 13:

items.text: A trade without a stop loss placed on the exchange.
Risking more than 2% on one trade.
Moving the stop loss away or removing it.
Averaging down or adding margin to a losing position.
A revenge trade after a loss.
A leveraged position left unattended without a stop loss while asleep or travelling.
Turning a losing trade into a long-term hold.
Trading with money I cannot afford to lose.

blocks.text: Two-factor authentication (2FA), a unique password and login alerts are enabled on the exchange account.
API keys are created with trading permission only and no withdrawal permission (and an IP restriction where possible).
Capital not needed for trading does not stay on the exchange; withdrawal addresses are whitelisted.
Exchanges carry risk too (hacks, withdrawal freezes, account blocks); where possible I do not keep all capital on one exchange.
When internet or power is unstable I do not open a new leveraged position. The stop loss always lives on the exchange itself.
I never give my private key or recovery phrase to anyone or any site. Signal sellers and unknown links are suspicious.
Long-term means spot, not futures (because of funding cost and liquidation risk).
Each asset has a written thesis, an invalidation condition and a weight cap (for example each altcoin at most 5% of the portfolio).
Entries and exits are scaled and reviewed every quarter.
The footprint of large investors (ETF flows, exchange reserves, Open Interest) is an input to analysis, not a reason to buy.
Daily (5 minutes): every trade of the day is completed in the journal.
Weekly (30 minutes): one repeated mistake and one rule to improve are identified.
Monthly (60 minutes): metrics are computed and thresholds (volume, R:R, risk) are tuned with data.
I judge a setup only after at least 30 trades.
Rules change only in a review session, never mid-trade and never after a loss.
A new setup is tested for 20 trades at risk 0.25% (or on demo).

refs.literal: A new setup is tested for 20 trades
refs.template: A new setup is tested for {v} trades

blocks.text: Red-line violation: the trade is closed at once, a 48 hour pause follows, and a one-paragraph report ("what happened, why, what I will do") is recorded in the journal.
After three violations in one month: risk 0.5% for 20 trades.
The main measure of monthly success is "rule compliance" (target 90% or more), not profit.

summary.thesis: All of your experience comes back to one principle: survive first, profit second. Every rule you wrote either prevents a big loss or prevents emotional behaviour.
summary.axesIntro: The lessons fall into four areas:

axes.title: Capital preservation
axes.text: Low leverage and margin, isolated mode, a take profit and a stop loss on every trade.

axes.title: Analysis before entry
axes.text: Trend, multiple timeframes, volume and divergence, news.

axes.title: Behaviour
axes.text: Patience, no emotion, staying away from greed and FOMO.

axes.title: Profit management
axes.text: Saving profit, going risk-free, realized profit, never abandoning an open position.

summary.lessonsIntro: Twelve lessons that come out of your notes:

lessons.text: Price rising on falling volume means caution, not entry.
Do not enter without a trend and without checking several timeframes.
No high leverage, small margin, always isolated.
Every trade has a take profit and a stop loss.
Buy and sell with Limit orders; do not buy with Market orders often.
The market moves in cycles: a price is seen several times, and if you are far in profit it is probably time to exit.
News (Federal Reserve, the Middle East, US politics) creates sharp swings; futures always with low leverage.
Behind every big unrealized profit sits a heavy loss; one dollar in hand beats ten thousand on paper.
After profit, go risk-free and raise the stop.
Do not abandon an open position; watch it.
After a big win, watch for the silent growth of your next trade's size.
Long-term investing means spot, not futures.

summary.keyInsights: Four points in your experience are worth more than the rest and have become rules in the constitution: the silent growth of position size after a win, "praying" inside a trade as a sign of having no plan, matching the target to the entry timeframe, and the difference between realized and paper profit.

review.intro: Five of your lessons need serious correction, the most important being leverage of 10 to 12; the rest are right and only need to become numeric and actionable. Each item has four parts: your experience, the correction, the reason, the fix.

items.title: Volume/price divergence
items.experience: Price rising on falling volume is a trick of exchanges and market makers; wait, look at another coin, and short after the reversal.
items.correction: This is "weak confirmation", not necessarily manipulation. Divergence does not tell the entry time and can last a while; seeing it is not a reason to short.
items.reason: You cannot measure a market maker's intent, but you can measure volume not agreeing with price. Shorting early in an uptrend is one of the most common ways to lose.
items.solution: Treat divergence as a "warning": entering in the direction of the big candle is forbidden until confirmation. Short only after a confirmed reversal (a structure break or a close below a key level), with half size and a clear stop. High funding and rising Open Interest next to divergence mean the longs are crowded.

items.title: Token volume and liquidity
items.experience: Volume should be neither too low nor too high, and it needs a parameter (for example a percentage).
items.correction: Two parameters are needed: absolute liquidity and relative volume.
items.reason: Low volume means slippage, wide spreads and easier stop hunts. An abnormal volume spike means news or crowding and sharp swings.
items.solution: Starting suggestion: futures volume over the last 24 hours of at least 100 million dollars, and relative volume (current volume ÷ 20-period average) between 0.7 and 3. Do not trade outside this range without a written reason. After 30 trades, tune the thresholds with the journal.

items.title: Trend and multiple timeframes
items.experience: Do not enter without considering the trend; look at the coin on several timeframes; do not scalp with a daily target.
items.correction: All three are right; they only need structure.
items.reason: A counter-trend trade has a lower chance of success and a wider stop. A daily target does not match a short-term entry and drags the trade into holding a loser.
items.solution: Three-timeframe model: direction (daily or 4 hour), setup (1 hour), entry (15 or 5 minutes). Define the trend by structure (higher or lower highs and lows) and the 50 and 200 EMA; for altcoins also check the bitcoin trend. The trade type (scalp, intraday, swing) is recorded before entry and does not change afterwards.

items.title: Placing orders
items.experience: Buy at the cheapest price, sell at the highest, and do not buy with Market orders often.
items.correction: You cannot know the bottom and top in advance. Make the goal "enter with a Limit order in a zone set in advance".
items.reason: Hunting for the best price misses good trades and then brings FOMO and chasing. Limit orders have lower fees (Maker) and less slippage.
items.solution: Scale in with 2 to 3 Limit orders in the zone. Market orders only for an emergency exit or an entry after a confirmed breakout. A missed trade is not a loss.

items.title: Leverage and margin
items.experience: Leverage at most 10 to 12 and margin at most 5 to 10% of equity.
items.correction: These numbers do not fit the "low leverage" you wrote elsewhere; 10 to 12 times is not low. The main measure is not leverage either but "risk per trade": the loss taken from equity when the stop is hit.
items.reason: At 10x leverage, a move of about 9.5% against the position liquidates it; in crypto, especially altcoins, a 10% move in one day or one news candle is not unusual. 10% margin at 12x leverage means a position of 120% of equity: a 5% stop means 6% of equity on one trade.
items.solution: Risk per trade 1% of equity; position size from the formula (article 3); default leverage 3 to 5 and an absolute cap of 10; liquidation price at least twice the stop distance from entry. Your 5 to 10% margin cap stays, as a second limit.

chart.caption: Approximate calculation for an isolated long at a 0.5% maintenance margin rate; the exact number is in the exchange calculator

items.after: The higher the leverage, the tighter the room for the stop; at 20x and 50x almost any normal swing hits it.

items.title: Isolated mode
items.experience: Always Isolated, so that a loss or liquidation only involves that position's margin.
items.correction: Right. Isolated caps the loss at the "position margin", but it does not replace a stop loss.
items.reason: Liquidation means losing the whole position margin, which is usually several times the 1% risk.
items.solution: Isolated plus a real stop loss. Adding margin to a losing position is forbidden, because it means refusing to accept the loss.

items.title: Take profit and stop loss
items.experience: Every trade must have a take profit and a stop loss.
items.correction: Right; two things are added: where the stop goes and the minimum reward-to-risk ratio (R:R).
items.reason: An arbitrary stop (for example "3%") has nothing to do with market structure and is easily hunted. With a poor R:R, even a high win rate loses.
items.solution: The stop goes behind the point that invalidates the trade idea (behind structure plus about 0.5 to 1 ATR), not on a round number. Minimum R:R is 1 to 1.5 and preferably 1 to 2. R means the initial risk of that trade; a 2R profit means twice what you risked. At 1 to 2 the breakeven win rate is about 33%, and at 1 to 1 it is 50%. The stop only moves toward profit and both orders are placed on the exchange at the moment of entry.

items.title: News and events
items.experience: The market is sensitive to news (Federal Reserve, the Middle East, US politics); futures always with low leverage, so the "liquidity price" goes down and news does not hit the trade.
items.correction: The correct term is liquidation price, and the goal is to move it "further" from the entry price: lower for a long, higher for a short. News has to be managed, not just endured.
items.reason: When news is released, spreads widen and stops fill with slippage. The distance to liquidation is your safety margin.
items.solution: Check the economic calendar every morning (Federal Reserve meeting, US inflation, employment data). From 30 minutes before to 60 minutes after a major event, open no new entry and keep open positions small or closed. On days of sudden news (such as regional tension), halve the risk.

items.title: Cycles, exiting deep in profit, going risk-free
items.experience: The market has cycles, and if you are far in profit it is time to exit; after a win go risk-free and move the stop to 50 to 70% of the profit; always save profit.
items.correction: The goal is right, but "a lot of profit" is not an exit criterion, and a stop at 50 to 70% of profit is tight for normal crypto swings. The exit rule must be written before entry.
items.reason: Closing winners early and holding losers ruins expectancy. A stop at entry or close to the profit is hit by a normal pullback and kills a good trade.
items.solution: Scaled exit: 50% of the position is closed at 1R to 1.5R and the stop on the rest goes to entry (plus fees); the rest stays with a trailing stop (structure or ATR) to the target. Locking 50 to 70% of profit only for moves above 3R. Use "cycles" like this: prices get retested, so enter on the retest and do not chase.

items.title: Silent growth of size after a win
items.experience: After a profitable trade, out of habit you put in a fixed percentage and the size keeps growing.
items.correction: An important insight; it only needs a written fix.
items.reason: Profit breeds false confidence ("the market's money"), and with leverage this cycle ends in a big loss.
items.solution: Size always comes from the 1% risk formula, not from a "fixed percentage" and habit. Check the account equity on the exchange before every entry and write it in the journal. After a big win, do not raise risk for 24 hours.

items.title: Patience, FOMO and watching the position
items.experience: Patience is the most important factor of survival; praying for more profit means getting close to liquidation; do not abandon an open position.
items.correction: Right; but "be emotionless" alone is not practical, and "be careful" should not turn into staring at the screen. Also, most losses come from high leverage, no stop loss and revenge trading, not only from market makers.
items.reason: Emotions are tamed by rules, not advice. Constant monitoring itself leads to overtrading and moving the stop.
items.solution: A cap of 3 trades a day; a 30 minute pause after each stop loss; the day ends after two consecutive stops. The "prayer rule": the moment you hope or pray, close half of the position. Watching means a live stop and target on the exchange, price alerts and set review hours; if you cannot monitor, do not open a position.

items.title: Large investors and spot
items.experience: BlackRock and ETFs take no risk and only enter to multiply; so buy long-term in spot, not futures.
items.correction: The conclusion (long-term = spot) is right, the premise is not. Institutions take risk too and manage it with diversification, weight caps and a long horizon. ETF entry is mostly a response to client demand, not a forecast that a token will multiply.
items.reason: If you treat institutional entry as a "signal to multiply", you follow them without judgement and may enter at the top.
items.solution: Take ETF flows, exchange reserves and Open Interest only as analysis inputs. For every long-term asset keep a written thesis, an invalidation condition and a weight cap (for example each altcoin at most 5% of the portfolio), and scale in and out.

items.title: Realized profit versus paper profit
items.experience: One dollar in hand beats ten thousand on paper; profit belongs in the wallet.
items.correction: Right; "realizing" only needs to become a set habit.
items.reason: Open profit can vanish in one candle, and capital left on an exchange also carries the risk of hacks, withdrawal freezes and account blocks.
items.solution: Each month move 30 to 50% of realized profit to spot or a personal wallet (default 30%).

additions.intro: Ten things were missing from your lessons without which the other rules do not last; the most important are fixed risk per trade and loss caps. The numbers are starting suggestions and should be tuned with your own journal data.

items.title: Fixed risk per trade
items.reason: Leverage and margin do not show the real loss; the loss at the moment the stop is hit does.
items.solution: 1% of equity (cap 2%); position size from the formula

items.title: Daily, weekly and drawdown loss caps
items.reason: Big drawdowns come from a chain of emotional losses, not from one loss.
items.solution: Daily 3%, weekly 6%, drawdown 10% from peak: stop and review

items.title: Position cap and correlation
items.reason: Several same-direction altcoins are in practice one position on bitcoin.
items.solution: At most 3 positions; total open risk at most 3%

items.title: Written setup
items.reason: Without a setup, every candle looks like an "opportunity".
items.solution: 1 to 2 setups with entry, invalidation and target conditions; no setup, no trade

items.title: Expectancy and statistics
items.reason: Win rate alone is misleading.
items.solution: Record the R of every trade; judge after 30 to 50 trades

items.title: Funding, fees and slippage
items.reason: Hidden costs turn short-term trading into a loser.
items.solution: Count fees and funding in R:R; do not hold a position that pays heavy funding for long

items.title: Operational and security risk
items.reason: Internet or power outages, hacks, withdrawal freezes and account blocks.
items.solution: Stop on the exchange; 2FA; API without withdrawal permission; no spare capital left on the exchange

items.title: Test before going live
items.reason: A new setup should not be discovered with real money.
items.solution: Demo or risk 0.25% for 20 trades

items.title: No averaging down and no moving the stop away
items.reason: The two common ways a small loss becomes a blown account.
items.solution: A red line in article 9

items.title: Journal and review
items.reason: Without data, learning from experience is guesswork.
items.solution: Record every trade; weekly and monthly review (journal section)

expectancy.title: Why win rate alone is not enough
expectancy.lead: The right measure is the expectancy of each trade in R:
expectancy.example: In this formula p is the win rate and R the reward-to-risk ratio. With a 40% win rate and an R:R of 1 to 2 we get 0.4 × 2 − 0.6 = 0.2; each trade earns 0.2R on average, even though 60% of trades lose.
expectancy.breakEvenNote: Breakeven win rate = 1 ÷ (1 + R); with R of 2 it is about 33% and with R of 1 it is 50%.

journal.intro: The journal does two jobs: before entry it stops rule-less trades, and after exit it shows repeated mistakes. The Excel journal sheet, with automatic formulas, comes separately with this document; this section explains its structure and quick template.
journal.flowCaption: The path of a trade · 7 steps, 1 decision, 1 improvement loop
journal.flowNote: If the checklist is not complete the trade is not opened; every closed trade goes into the journal and rules change only in the weekly or monthly review.

security.text: Two-factor authentication (2FA), a unique password and login alerts are enabled on the exchange account.
API keys are created with trading permission only and no withdrawal permission (and an IP restriction where possible).
Capital not needed for trading does not stay on the exchange; withdrawal addresses are whitelisted.
Exchanges carry risk too (hacks, withdrawal freezes, account blocks); where possible I do not keep all capital on one exchange.
When internet or power is unstable I do not open a new leveraged position. The stop loss always lives on the exchange itself.
I never give my private key or recovery phrase to anyone or any site. Signal sellers and unknown links are suspicious.

adviceOfDay.text: Price rising on falling volume means caution, not entry.
Do not enter without a trend and without checking several timeframes.
No high leverage, small margin, always isolated.
Every trade has a take profit and a stop loss.
Buy and sell with Limit orders; do not buy with Market orders often.
The market moves in cycles: a price is seen several times, and if you are far in profit it is probably time to exit.
News (Federal Reserve, the Middle East, US politics) creates sharp swings; futures always with low leverage.
Behind every big unrealized profit sits a heavy loss; one dollar in hand beats ten thousand on paper.
After profit, go risk-free and raise the stop.
Do not abandon an open position; watch it.
After a big win, watch for the silent growth of your next trade's size.
Long-term investing means spot, not futures.
My first goal is survival, my second is profit. As long as there is capital, there is another chance.
A good trade is one taken by the rules, not one that made money. A loss within the rules is a cost of doing business.
The market is indifferent to me. Only three things are in my control: position size, exit point and my own behaviour.
Not trading is a decision too. No setup, no trade.
A missed trade is not a loss and I do not chase it.
The stop only moves toward profit; it is never moved further away or removed.
Averaging down on a losing position and adding margin to it are forbidden.
I do not turn a loss into a "long-term investment".
Profit is profit only once it is realized; open profit is just a number on the screen.
When I am deep in profit and want "more", I close part of it at once; greed is a signal.
Revenge trading and trading to recover a loss are forbidden.
Prayer rule: if I catch myself hoping or praying, it means I have no plan; I close half of the position.
I do not look for someone else to blame for a loss; first I check which rule I broke.

ui.onb.welcome.title: Welcome to Andarz
ui.onb.welcome.body: Andarz enforces your own trading constitution: before entry it stops rule-less trades, and after exit it shows your repeated mistakes.
ui.onb.privacy.title: Your data stays on your phone
ui.onb.privacy.body: The journal works offline and sends no data. You create and keep the encrypted backup yourself; if you lose its password, no one can recover it.
ui.onb.how.title: How Andarz works
ui.onb.how.1: Before entry: the eight-item checklist and the position-size calculation; if any limit fails, entry stays closed and the reason is written with numbers.
ui.onb.how.2: During the trade: the stop only moves toward profit and violations are recorded.
ui.onb.how.3: After exit: R, rule compliance and the main mistake are recorded, and weekly and monthly statistics are built from them.
